title: What outlasts the ledger
excerpt: The institutions the founding family established are not a line item. A short reflection on stewardship, and on the buildings that keep working long after the ribbon is cut.
body: Every enterprise eventually produces two kinds of record. There is the one that is audited, and there is the one made up of the things that are still standing and still in use after the people who built them have gone.

The second record is harder to keep and harder to value. It does not appear on a balance sheet, and it is only legible at a distance of decades, by which point nobody is in a position to take credit for it.

Institutions are the clearest instance. A building put up for a school or a hospital enters a life of its own the moment it is handed over. It is used in ways nobody predicted, altered by people who never met the architect, and judged — fairly — on whether it still works.

That is a demanding standard and it is the right one. Work of this kind is not finished at completion. It is finished, if it ever is, when a generation that had no part in commissioning it finds it serviceable.
